briefs.headline: Abhishek's 30-ball ton hid the number that should really worry T20 bowlers
briefs.deck: Abhishek Sharma's 30-ball T20I hundred against Afghanistan was spectacular, but the bigger story lies in the numbers around it. The India opener is striking at 194.55 while averaging 33.18, combining extraordinary aggression with consistency. His powerplay dominance, six-hitting, record-breaking numbers and the costly downside of his approach reveal how his game has evolved.
briefs.bodyText:
The 30-ball ton was, oddly, the least surprising part of what 
Abhishek Sharma
 did at the Arun Jaitley Stadium. It isn't even his fastest hundred. What's odd about the innings is what it says about the number sitting next to that extraordinary strike rate: his average.
Somewhere in 
Abhishek
 Sharma's memory, though, there's a faster century still. It came two years ago, for Punjab against Meghalaya in a Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy fixture nobody outside domestic cricket was watching: 28 balls, no fanfare.
So when he reached three figures in 30 deliveries against Afghanistan in New Delhi, becoming the fastest T20I centurion ever produced by a Full Member nation and only the third-fastest in the format's history overall, it wasn't a discovery. It was a confirmation, delivered on a bigger stage, of something the data had already been saying for a while.
Abhishek Sharma scores in the India vs Afghanistan T2OI series
The ground has some history with him already. Eight years earlier, on the same square when it was still called Feroz Shah Kotla, a 17-year-old Sharma walked out at number six for Delhi Daredevils against Royal Challengers Bangalore and top-scored on IPL debut — an unbeaten 46 off 19 balls. It was the innings that first put his name into circulation.
None of that is really the story, though. The story is what his average has been doing while all this has been going on.
The average, not the strike rate
After 58 T20I innings, Abhishek averages 33.18 at a strike rate of 194.55. Among those who have batted at least 20 times in T20Is since Abhishek's debut in July 2024, nobody has struck as quickly as his 194.55 per 100 balls.
Abhishek Sharma fast and consistent not fast or consistent
Put that alongside the numbers of his closest opening peers and the combination starts to look strange. Phil Salt, across almost the same number of innings, averages 34.34 at 165.89: a fraction higher on average, nearly thirty runs per hundred balls slower. Finn Allen's numbers read 28.67 and 170.74; Travis Head's, 28.40 and 156.69. Multiply strike rate by average and divide by 100 and you get a rough figure for scoring speed without giving up the average: Abhishek comes out at 64.56, against 56.97 for Salt, 48.95 for Allen and 44.50 for Head.
The gap isn't really about six-hitting or bravado. It's that T20 cricket generally punishes extreme aggression with a lower average, and in Abhishek's case, over more than fifty innings now, it hasn't.
Where the runs actually come from
Look closer and the shape of his batting explains some of it. Of his 1,858 T20I runs, 1,484 (79.9%) have come in boundaries. In the Afghanistan innings that figure spiked to 94.44%, the highest boundary share recorded in any men's T20I century.
A six every 7.58 balls
He hits a six in T20Is every 7.58 balls, comfortably ahead of Allen (8.47), Salt (12.47) and Head (14.20). Zoom out to his whole T20 career, across formats, and he reached his hundredth six faster, by balls faced, than anyone the format has seen, edging West Indies' Evin Lewis. Among Indian batters with 50 or more T20 sixes, nobody has matched his rate of clearing the boundary. He's the best of the lot, streets ahead of Sanju Samson, Shivam Dube, Suryakumar Yadav and 
Yuvraj Singh
, the mentor whose fastest-fifty record he's now threatened on at least three occasions.
Most sixes for India in a T2OI match
The clearest expression of the method is the powerplay. His strike rate in an innings' first ten balls, 176, is the joint-highest on record, level with Tim David: he isn't feeling out the pitch before he attacks. His boundary percentage inside the powerplay, 33.48% according to CricViz, is the best among batters with 500-plus T20I runs.
Abhishek owns India's big Powerplays
This has happened before, too. India have breached 90 in a T20I powerplay four times, and Abhishek has been the one doing the damage on every occasion: 59 not out off 21 against England at the Wankhede last year, 51 not out off 14 against New Zealand in Guwahati this year, 51 off 19 in the World Cup final in Ahmedabad, where he reached fifty in 18 balls under the most pressure he's likely ever faced. His 76 not out off 22 balls is simply the largest number yet on that list. His opening stand with Samson, 142 off 59 balls, is now the fastest century opening partnership for India in T20Is by run rate, overtaking a stand between KL Rahul and Rohit Sharma from Indore in 2017.
What it costs him
None of this comes free. Abhishek walked into this year's T20 World Cup and made three consecutive ducks, followed that with 15, 10 and 9, and salvaged the campaign with two match-defining fifties, one in a must-win Super Eight game against Zimbabwe, the other in the final. Eight innings, 141 runs, an average of 17.62. "As a batter, as a cricketer, sometimes [my form is] going to go up and down," he said afterwards, and there's little sense he sees the ducks as a separate problem from the sixes. They're the same bet, landing differently.
What this approach costs Abhishek 
And 2026 has underlined that cost. Abhishek has been dismissed for a duck 10 times in T20 cricket this calendar year, the most by any batter in a year, ahead of Rashid Khan's nine in 2019 and Shadab Khan's nine in 2024. Five of those have come off the first ball, making him the joint-most prolific first-ball duck-maker in a calendar year in T20Is, alongside Rwanda's Kevin Irakoze in 2023 and Richard Ngarava in 2024.
What's changed isn't the risk-taking. It's how deliberately he manages it. Against the Rashid Khan, Mohammad Nabi and Mujeeb Ur Rahman spin trio in the Afghanistan series, he made a conscious tactical switch, going only forward or down the pitch, never back, and scored 54 off 15 against them, including 4, 4, 6 off three straight Rashid deliveries in the last over of the powerplay.
In the first two games, camped on the back foot against the same bowlers, he'd managed only 29 off 17. "It's always about me backing my shots because I don't have a lot of shots," he said earlier this year, after an 85 off 34 against New Zealand, which sounds like modesty until you notice how precisely that limited toolkit is being aimed.
Level with Kohli
Most T20 centuries by Indians
This is now his tenth century in all forms of T20 cricket, level with Virat Kohli for the most by an Indian batter, and his third T20I hundred, level with Samson, and behind only Rohit Sharma and Suryakumar Yadav in India's own list. The number worth sitting with isn't the 30 balls. It's how Abhishek has managed to keep his average above 30 while scoring at a strike rate of nearly 195.

briefs.headline: From cleaning rest rooms to winning two Asian Games golds — the rise of Aslam Inamdar
briefs.deck: The star raider has cleared many hurdles and come a long way since taking to kabaddi when he was about 14; irrespective of the hardships, the sport has been a constant
briefs.bodyText:
There was a moment in the second half of the Asian Games kabaddi gold-medal match against Iran when Aslam Inamdar made a daring raid deep into the opposition half.
His teammate Pawan Sehrawat groaned inwardly as he did so. India’s lead was narrow. Iran was still in the contest. It was a risk that could have gone badly wrong. “It was a bad decision,” Pawan would say later. But Inamdar made the dash count, securing two touches and emerging unscathed. The points brought India closer to victory. “It was a wrong move, but ant bhala toh sab bhala (if the end is good, it’s all worth it),” Inamdar said after the match.
He grinned when he recalled the sequence later. It had been a tough decision to make. Wasn’t he worried when he made that move? What would have happened if it had gone wrong? “Bhai, I’ve gone through things you wouldn’t even imagine. This is nothing,” he said.
That, in many ways, is the story of Aslam Inamdar.
There was a time when, as a 14-year-old, he travelled across Maharashtra in search of kabaddi tournaments without even having enough money for a train ticket. He slept under train seats, survived on stale vada pav or whatever food was available at tournaments. He sometimes stuffed leftover food which often spilled into his bag. “If there was work to be done, I did it. I’ve cleaned toilets. I’ve sold juice and made tea. I’ve worked in fields. If there was a kabaddi tournament to play, I found a way to get there.”
In Nagoya on Saturday, Inamdar stood on the mat as India beat Iran to win the men’s kabaddi gold. It is his second Asian Games gold medal. The distance between those two versions of Inamdar is difficult even for him to comprehend.
“It still feels like a dream to me,” he said. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home holds two international medals.”
The medals are the latest chapter in a journey that began at Takli Bhan in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar district, where Inamdar grew up as one of five children.
His father passed away when he was young, leaving his mother to raise the family. She worked in other homes, doing household chores and washing utensils, to keep the family going. Later, his elder brother Waseem joined the police force and took responsibility, including helping arrange the marriages of their two sisters.
Money was scarce. Inamdar remembers growing up in a house without proper flooring or roof. There were times when even food was difficult to come by.
So, he learnt early that work meant survival. At 11 or 12, he collected discarded bottles and sold them to scrap dealers to buy food. Later, he worked at tea stalls and juice bars, washed utensils, cleaned washrooms and worked in farm fields. He admits he stole sometimes. “It was just to fill my stomach. I faced many hard situations without letting them break me,” he said.
Through all of it, there was one constant: kabaddi. Waseem was a well-known player across several districts while senior player Rahul Bhor also inspired him. Inamdar wanted to establish his own identity. “No matter how long I worked during the day or night, I always went to the ground to train,” the raider said.
Kabaddi was a sport he could afford. It required little equipment, and the village ground was enough. For a boy with very little money, it offered something priceless: a chance. By the time he was 14 or 15, Inamdar was travelling alone to tournaments to compete in the 50kg and 55kg categories. He earned between ₹200 and ₹500 a match.
The money was little, but it mattered. It bought him meals when he might otherwise have gone hungry. More importantly, it kept him moving from one tournament to the next.
The path was neither smooth nor uninterrupted. In 2014, while India competed at the Asian Games, Inamdar was at home nursing a fractured leg and following kabaddi on television. His life at the time seemed a world away from an international career. “I was just watching kabaddi on TV. But I believe God’s plans are always better. My hard work never stopped.”
He kept working. Eventually, the Pro Kabaddi League changed the scale of his life.
In his first season, he earned ₹8 lakh. For someone who had once struggled to put food on the table, the money was almost incomprehensible. “Eight lakh felt like eight crore to me,” he said.
He did not forget where he had come from. With his first major earnings, he bought a gold necklace for his mother. Kabaddi had given him something that had once seemed almost impossible: financial security, recognition and a career. He went on to captain Puneri Paltan and establish himself as one of India’s leading players.
Then came the international medals. Inamdar won his first Asian Games gold in Hangzhou. Three years later in Nagoya, he has another. And once again, the final was against Iran — the one opponent which has consistently pushed India hardest at the Asian Games. “Iran is generally the most challenging opponent for us,” Inamdar said. “It has a strong defence and has very experienced players like Fazel Atrachali, who played in his fifth Asian Games.”
For Inamdar, beating such a formidable opponent made the gold more meaningful. “A tough challenge makes winning the gold medal feel even more rewarding.”
But for Inamdar, the significance of the medal lies beyond the result. It is the culmination of a journey that began when he was a boy travelling across Maharashtra for a few hundred rupees, when he collected scrap bottles for food and worked whatever jobs he could find before heading to the kabaddi ground.
Today, he tries to pass on that experience to younger players.
At his training ground in Thane, he speaks to juniors, particularly those from underprivileged backgrounds, about his own journey. He wants them to understand that difficult circumstances do not have to determine where they end up. “I want young, underprivileged players to dream big and aim to achieve even more than I have. I want them to know that whatever happens, they shouldn’t stop working hard. They shouldn’t stop believing,” he said.

briefs.headline: Chess Olympiad: India wins silver in Open section; women claim bronze
briefs.bodyText:
The men won the silver, and the women the bronze. India, the defending champion in both the open and women’s sections, could not repeat the stunning twin success of 2024, but at least finished with team medals at the Chess Olympiad.
In the open section, host Uzbekistan emerged as the champion, while China came up with a dominant show to win the women’s title despite not fielding some of its best players. On the final day, the Indian men drew with Hungary 2-2, while the women shared the honours with Georgia (2-2).
The Indian men finished with 18 points, two less than the host, which defeated Ukraine 2.5-1.5. Germany, which surprised many, won the bronze after its 2.5-1.5 win over the Netherlands.
Arjun Erigaisi’s win over Peter Leko on the second board proved crucial, as D. Gukesh was beaten by Gleb Dudin. R. Praggnanandhaa and Nihal Sarin drew their games.
For the Indian women, Koneru Humpy scored a significant win on the top board against Nana Dzagnidge. Though Divya Deshmukh lost on the second board, to Bela Khotenashvili, Vantika Agrawal and the magnificent B. Savitha Shri both drew their games to ensure India would end up on the podium, after all.
India also retained the Gaprindashvili Trophy, given to the team with the best overall score. India is the only country to win a medal in both open and women’s sections.
India also won a slew of board medals. Savitha struck gold on the reserve board in the women’s section, in which Divya won the silver on the third board. Humpy and Vantika won bronze on the top board and fourth board respectively. In the open section, Gukesh won silver on the fourth board, while Praggnanandhaa claimed the bronze on the top board.

briefs.headline: IND vs WI 1st ODI: Kohli, Gill ace the chase after Kuldeep’s heroics
briefs.deck: Kohli completed his 15,000 ODI runs during his record-extending century and remained unbeaten on 139 off only 88 balls (10 fours, 9 sixes) as India scored 300/2 in 41.4 overs in reply to the West Indies’ 295/7
briefs.bodyText:
This charmingly laidback city is known for its beaches caressed by the blue Arabian Sea. On Sunday, there was another sea of blue that filled the stands of the Greenfield Stadium. And those Indian fans were treated to a fascinating day, and night, of cricket.
They got to see some sparkling strokeplay from their favourite batters and to witness a major historic feat, too. They could also celebrate an easy win for India, despite being set a competitive target in the first ODI.
India went past the West Indies’ 295 for seven with eight wickets and 8.2 overs to spare, to go 1-0 up in the three-match series. Skipper Shubman Gill (110, 108b, 13x4, 1x6) and Virat Kohli (139 not out, 88b, 10x4, 9x6) turned the chase into a walk in the park, as they destroyed the Caribbean bowlers with flair and finesse. And there were some delectable shots from Rohit Sharma too, though he wasn’t in the best of touch.
And it was a special day for Kohli for another reason, as he crossed 15,000 runs in ODI cricket. Only the other Indian master, Sachin Tendulkar, has climbed that mountain.
When he swivel-pulled Alzarri Joseph for a four through mid-wicket, the crowd cheered loudly, as if reminding the great man that he had indeed reached that milestone; he raised his hands in acknowledgement and even allowed himself a smile. It was only fitting that Gill was at the other end, to whom he had passed the baton of the great Indian batting tradition, which he had received from Tendulkar.
Kohli had joined Gill at the fall of Rohit’s wicket. Joseph had frustrated the Mumbai stylist by bowling a series of dot balls at him in a row and then making him play straight to the deep-midwicket fielder. The opening stand was worth 74 in 12 overs.
Gill, who had been dropped by substitute Keemo Paul off Jayden Seales, and Kohli killed whatever hopes Shai Hope’s men may have entertained with their 151-run partnership off just 132 balls for the second wicket. After the captain departed, the former captain continued to go after the bowling as if there was no tomorrow, and brought up his 55th ODI century with a towering six off Gudakesh Motie over long-on.
Kohli’s masterclass put into the background a fine hundred by the West Indies opener Justin Greaves (101, 108b, 12x4) and a brilliant spell of spin bowling by Kuldeep Yadav, whose four wickets restricted the visitors after a first-wicket stand of 135.

briefs.headline: 'I promised myself': Virat Kohli after 15,000-run landmark
briefs.deck: Virat Kohli became only the second batter after Sachin Tendulkar to complete 15,000 ODI runs. He also hit his record-extending 55th ODI century as India beat West Indies by eight wickets in the first ODI. Kohli said his priority has always been to understand the situation and do what the team needs.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Virat Kohli
 reached another major ODI milestone on Sunday, but the star batter made it clear that records and numbers have never been his main focus.
Kohli became only the second batter after 
Sachin Tendulkar
 to complete 15,000 ODI runs. He also hit his record-extending 55th ODI century as India beat West Indies by eight wickets in the first ODI.
Kohli wants to keep pushing himself
Kohli said his priority has always been to understand the situation and do what the team needs.
"My focus has never really been on these milestones, so to say. It's just understanding the situation along the course of just doing the job for the team, (the) achievements come along," Kohli told the broadcaster after the match.
Kohli smashed nine sixes and 10 fours to remain unbeaten on 139 off 88 balls. India scored 300 for two in 41.4 overs while chasing West Indies' 295 for seven.
"Obviously, I feel very grateful and very blessed to be in this position for having played for so long. Just keeping my head down, working hard and thanking God for everything that I've been blessed with and the opportunities that I've got in my life to be where I am," Kohli said.
"We have a very blessed life and a blessed journey because so many people want to be here, but we get to be the lucky ones, so we better put our head down and just work hard every day of our lives," he added.
A new challenge at this stage
Kohli said becoming more aggressive with the bat and playing at a higher gear has been a challenge for him at this stage of his career.
"… just the understanding of your game, firstly. Also, at the stage that I'm at, just keeping myself physically very fit because the game's more or less in the mind. I've never been a guy who practised a lot even when I was playing all three formats as you know," he replied to a query from former India coach Ravi Shastri.
"For me it's about about staying mentally fresh, staying in the present moment and just expressing myself really out there to play in a certain way, get used to this template more often."
"I got a challenge at this stage of my career to kind of up the ante and play a gear or two higher and yeah, that was exciting for me to work on."
He continued, "Again, it excites you when you have to unlock a new version at this stage of your career, which will eventually help any team that you play for, be it playing for India or in the IPL. It's really helped me a lot to play with a free mind and I think that's what's working for me."
Fitness helps him play with a free mind
Kohli also spoke about the role of fitness in his batting and how it helps him visualise his game.
"I think to follow a free mind, you need a fit body so for me, it works the other way around. I stay physically fit and then I'm able to visualise the game in the way that I want to play, which allows me the best chance to go out there and execute in the way that I did tonight," he said.
He also stressed the importance of remembering the journey that brought him to this stage.
"I think the only thing we need to do is just look back once and where we came from. That's something that we tend to forget when we are caught up with the hustle of the world and the positions we get into with so much attention and fame and so much love from the fans" he said.
"It can be very easy to forget where you came from. But just looking back at the journey from when you started as a child just makes you feel grateful."
Kohli added, "I enjoy each and every minute that I'm out there playing for India because I understand that, as I said I could have been a possibility that I wouldn't be standing here. I wouldn't have played for India at all."
World Cup goal is clear
The 37-year-old said playing only one format for India has also given him clarity about what he wants to achieve.
"We are a year away from the World Cup. I know what my goal is and it's pretty clear for me that whatever games we get, I just need to keep working on different aspects of the game, keep myself physically fit, challenge myself to be out there."
"… run from boundary to boundary in the last 15 overs if I can, field in the inner ring, show intensity. If I keep ticking all those boxes, I've got some time left to play in this format as well."
"So when I get an opportunity, I feel happy rather than feeling anxiety or pressure to make the most of it. I just want to express myself and play my game. As I said, I promised myself I'm going to play positively because I can."
"I'm going to continue to play like that but not be reckless. There's a fine line, which as a professional, as an experienced player, I should have the ability to execute in this way without playing reckless shots and get the team through," he added.

briefs.headline: 1st ODI: Virat, Shubman centuries power India to 8-wicket win over West Indies
briefs.deck: Virat Kohli scored his 55th ODI century while Shubman Gill contributed a solid hundred. India chased down the 295-run target with ease in Thiruvananthapuram. Kuldeep Yadav took four wickets to stifle the West Indies' batting effort. Justin Greaves made a maiden ODI century, but his efforts were insufficient. The match showcased India's dominance in One Day Internationals on home soil.
briefs.bodyText:
THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: 
Virat Kohli
 brought up his record 55th ODI century with an emphatic six, marching past 15,000 runs in this format. India captain 
Shubman Gill
 also looked imperious, as he reached his 10th ODI hundred by unfurling his signature cuts and drives. Between them, India cantered to an 8-wicket win here at the Greenfield International Stadium in a chase that never once felt like a contest.
A brilliant opening salvo from 
Rohit Sharma
, whose 35-ball 32 laid the foundation for India’s pursuit, as the hosts eased past the 295-run target in 41.4 overs against a lacklustre West Indies bowling attack. India’s insouciance with the bat came after a clinical display from Kuldeep Yadav, his wrist-spin ripping through the West Indies middle-order with a four-wicket haul. This match was a lesson in class, distance and everything in between.
Gill and Kohli put together a 151-run stand for the second wicket that had the Thiruvananthapuram crowd on its feet, and for a while it looked like the two of them would see the chase home between them. Cramps and fatigue got the better of Gill, as he eventually walked off, his 110 off 108 balls, with 13 fours and a six, a knock that had class written through it. 
Kohli, still chasing down whatever he considers “unfinished business” before the 2027 World Cup, was unbeaten on a scarcely believable 88-ball 139 in the end, his tenth ODI ton against the West Indies.
West Indies didn’t have much to show for in the afternoon, but they did have Justin Greaves. Asked to bat first, the visitors leaned almost entirely on their opener, who cracked a maiden ODI hundred, 101 off 108 balls, to drag the visitors to 295/7. He put on 135 for the first wicket with John Campbell, who chipped in with a breezy 62 off 60, and that stand alone was worth the price of admission: West Indies’ first century opening partnership in ODIs in two years.
Just when the West Indies looked like running away with the game, Kuldeep spun a web with figures of 10-1-40-4. It was a tour-de-force performance by India’s virtuoso chinaman bowler who was playing a different contest to the rest of his teammates.
After a string of wide deliveries that left West Indies batter John Campbell visibly tetchy, Kuldeep dropped one full and straight at the stumps. On cue, Campbell got provoked and went for a mistimed sweep that was picked up by Prasidh Krishna at backward square-leg. Kuldeep then conned West Indies captain Shai Hope with drift, eliciting a leading edge that ballooned towards Ravindra Jadeja at cover.
Kuldeep’s most telling blow was the manner in which he dismissed opener Justin Greaves, who was trapped lbw after missing a sweep against a ball on a length on leg stump. Greaves’ departure set jitters in the visitors’ dressing room, and on the next delivery, the Kanpur spinner bamboozled Jewel Andrew with a googly to prise his fourth scalp.
Kuldeep’s timely blows meant the West Indies would lose their momentum in the middle overs, capping a redemption for the 31-year-old, who endured a tepid Sri Lanka Test series. Whatever Kuldeep lost in Sri Lanka, he’s found it again in Thiruvananthapuram.

briefs.headline: Following court order, JKCA holds annual general meeting, discusses Irani Cup
briefs.deck: The court directed that any decision taken at the AGM ‘shall not be declared’
briefs.bodyText:
Mired in legal wranglings, the J&K Cricket Association (JKCA) held its Annual General Meeting (AGM) in Jammu on Sunday (September 27, 2026) after a gap of nearly 10 years and discussed the hosting of the Irani Cup being held for the first time in Kashmir from October 1 to 5. The AGM went ahead following a court order on September 26.
A JKCA spokesman said 15 authorised club members, office bearers, and members of the Association participated, adding: “they discussed preparations for the Irani Cup, scheduled to be held at the Sher-e-Kashmir Stadium, Srinagar, from October 1 to 5, 2026.”
“The meeting stressed the importance of unity, collective responsibility, and a positive approach among all stakeholders to further strengthen and promote cricket across J&K. The members expressed their commitment to working together to build on recent achievements and take J&K cricket to greater heights,” the spokesman said.
A local court in Jammu in a ruling on Saturday (September 26, 2026) permitted the JKCA to hold the AGM. Javed Ahmad Kitab, who was suspended in July this year as president of the JKCA, had petitioned the court with a claim that he was still “the elected president of the JKCA”. His suspension through a resolution this year was followed by the constitution and functioning of the Apex Council and appointment of an Ombudsman.
Hearing the petition filed by Mr. Kitab, the court considered pleas challenging the JKCA notice and alleged non-compliance with provisions of the JKCA Constitution, but allowed the AGM. The court, however, directed that any decision taken at the proposed AGM “shall not be declared and shall remain subject to the outcome of the interim application”. The matter is listed for further proceedings on October 10.
Meanwhile, the court was also informed that the JKCA election conducted on January 16, 2026, whose results were subsequently declared on May 21, 2026, “was contrary to the rules and regulations of the Association and that several clubs and their representatives, who had participated in earlier working committee and election meetings, were deprived of their alleged right to participate and vote”.
